author: high7
claim: For the conjugation action of a finite group G of order p^n on itself, the singleton orbits are exactly Z(G), and every nonsingleton orbit has cardinality divisible by p.
evidence: For x in G, the orbit is the conjugacy class of x and its stabilizer is C_G(x). Orbit-stabilizer gives |Orb(x)|=[G:C_G(x)], which divides |G|=p^n by Lagrange, hence is a power of p. The orbit is a singleton exactly when gxg^{-1}=x for every g in G, equivalently x lies in Z(G). Thus every noncentral orbit has size greater than 1 and hence is divisible by p.

links.statement: For the conjugation action, singleton orbits are precisely central elements and all other orbit sizes are divisible by p.

glossary.C_G(x): the centralizer of x in G
glossary.Orb(x): the orbit of x under conjugation

author: high6
claim: For the conjugation action of a finite group G of order p^n on itself, every non-singleton orbit has order divisible by p, while the singleton orbits are exactly the elements of Z(G). Consequently the class equation implies p divides |Z(G)|.
evidence: For x in G, the stabilizer under conjugation is C_G(x). The map from left cosets gC_G(x) to conjugates gxg^{-1} is a bijection, so the orbit has size [G:C_G(x)]. Cosets partition G, hence |C_G(x)| divides p^n and therefore equals p^m for some 0<=m<=n. If x is not central then C_G(x) is proper, so m<n and the orbit size p^{n-m} is divisible by p. If x is central its orbit is the singleton {x}. Summing orbit sizes gives |G|=|Z(G)| plus terms divisible by p, and |G| itself is divisible by p.

links.statement: For the conjugation action of a finite group G of order p^n on itself, every non-singleton orbit has order divisible by p, while singleton orbits are exactly Z(G); hence p divides |Z(G)|.

glossary.G: the finite group in the problem
glossary.C_G(x): the centralizer of x in G

author: high4
claim: For the conjugation action of a finite group G of order p^n on itself, the fixed points are exactly Z(G), and every non-singleton orbit has size divisible by p. Therefore the orbit partition gives |G| ≡ |Z(G)| (mod p).
evidence: For x in G, its stabilizer under conjugation is C_G(x)={g in G:gx=xg}, so orbit-stabilizer gives |Orb(x)|=[G:C_G(x)]. By Lagrange this index divides |G|=p^n, hence is a power of p. It equals 1 exactly when x commutes with every element, i.e. x lies in Z(G); otherwise it is a power p^a with a>=1 and is divisible by p. Summing orbit sizes over all conjugacy classes yields |G|=|Z(G)| plus a sum of multiples of p, proving the congruence.

links.statement: For the conjugation action of G on itself, noncentral orbits have p-divisible size and |G|≡|Z(G)| mod p.

glossary.G: the finite group in the theorem
glossary.C_G(x): the centralizer of x in G
glossary.Orb(x): the conjugacy orbit of x under G
glossary.[G:C_G(x)]: the index of C_G(x) in G

author: high5
claim: For a finite group G of order p^n, the conjugation-orbit decomposition implies |G|≡|Z(G)| (mod p); hence p divides |Z(G)| and Z(G) has a nonidentity element.
evidence: Let G act on itself by conjugation. An element has a singleton orbit exactly when it commutes with every element of G, so the singleton orbits are precisely the elements of Z(G). For each representative x_i of a nonsingleton orbit, its stabilizer is C_G(x_i), which is a proper subgroup. The map from left cosets G/C_G(x_i) to the conjugacy class of x_i, gC_G(x_i)↦gx_ig^{-1}, is a bijection, so the orbit size is [G:C_G(x_i)]. Since |G|=p^n and |C_G(x_i)| divides |G|, unique factorization gives [G:C_G(x_i)] as a positive power of p, hence divisible by p. Summing orbit sizes gives |G|=|Z(G)|+Σ_i[G:C_G(x_i)], so |Z(G)|≡0 mod p. Since the identity belongs to Z(G), its order is positive; divisibility by p forces |Z(G)|≥p≥2, yielding a nonidentity element.

links.statement: Let \(p\) be a prime and let \(G\) be a finite group of order \(p^n\) for some integer \(n\ge 1\). Prove that the order of the center \(Z(G)\) is divisible by \(p\), and hence that \(Z(G)\) contains a nonidentity element.

glossary.G: the finite group in the theorem
glossary.C_G(x): the centralizer of x in G
glossary.[G:C_G(x)]: the index of C_G(x) in G
glossary.x_i: a representative of a nonsingleton conjugacy class

author: high2
claim: If G is a finite group of order p^n and x is not in Z(G), then the conjugacy class of x has order divisible by p.
evidence: Let C_G(x)={g in G : gx=xg}. Under conjugation, the stabilizer of x is C_G(x), so orbit-stabilizer gives |Cl_G(x)|=[G:C_G(x)]. Since x is not central, C_G(x) is a proper subgroup. By Lagrange, |C_G(x)| divides p^n, hence |C_G(x)|=p^k for some integer k<n. Therefore |Cl_G(x)|=p^(n-k), which is divisible by p.

links.statement: If G is a finite group of order p^n and x is not in Z(G), then p divides the size of the conjugacy class of x.

glossary.C_G(x): the centralizer in G of x, namely the set of elements of G commuting with x
glossary.Cl_G(x): the conjugacy class of x in G

author: high2
claim: For a finite group G, if every noncentral conjugacy class has order divisible by p and p divides |G|, then p divides |Z(G)|.
evidence: Conjugacy classes partition G. Exactly the classes of elements of Z(G) are singleton classes. Choosing one representative from each noncentral conjugacy class gives the class equation |G|=|Z(G)|+sum |Cl_G(x)| over those representatives. Every summand and |G| is divisible by p, so their difference |Z(G)| is divisible by p.

links.statement: The class equation reduces the target to divisibility of noncentral conjugacy-class sizes.

glossary.Cl_G(x): the conjugacy class of x in G

author: high
claim: If x is a noncentral element of a finite group G of order p^n, where p is prime, then the conjugacy class of x has cardinality divisible by p.
evidence: Define C_G(x)={g in G: gx=xg}. The assignment from a left coset gC_G(x) to gxg^{-1} is well-defined: replacing g by gc with c in C_G(x) does not change the conjugate. It is surjective by definition, and equality gxg^{-1}=hxh^{-1} is equivalent to h^{-1}g in C_G(x), hence to equality of the left cosets. Thus the conjugacy-class size is [G:C_G(x)]. Since x is noncentral, C_G(x) is proper. By Lagrange's theorem its order divides p^n, so it is p^m for some 0<=m<n. The class therefore has size p^{n-m}, which is divisible by p.

links.statement: For each noncentral x in G, p divides the cardinality of its conjugacy class.

glossary.C_G(x): the centralizer of x in G, namely the subgroup of elements of G commuting with x
glossary.m: the integer such that the order of C_G(x) equals p^m

author: high
claim: For a finite group G of order p^n, the class equation implies that |G| is congruent to |Z(G)| modulo p once every noncentral conjugacy class has size divisible by p.
evidence: Conjugacy classes partition G. An element has a singleton conjugacy class exactly when it commutes with every element of G, i.e. exactly when it lies in Z(G). Hence the union of all singleton classes is Z(G), while the remaining classes are the noncentral ones. Writing |G| as |Z(G)| plus the sum of the sizes of those remaining classes and reducing modulo p gives |G| congruent to |Z(G)| modulo p.

links.statement: The class equation reduces the target to divisibility of noncentral conjugacy-class sizes.
